The terms this manual uses, defined once. Short definitions of the words the Aertun manual and console use: sources, events, detections, findings, cases, regimes, playbooks, actions, the audit log. SourceWhere events come from: a connector reading another tool's API, a log file mapped by a source mapping, or a feed another system pushes to. EventOne thing that happened, mapped to one shape and kept append-only in the event store before anything reads it. Detection ruleA declared condition over events, with fixtures it must match and must not. A rule is live, in the trial ring (it records what it would raise) or off. FindingSomething a rule, a correlation or an automation says is wrong. Its state is open, triaged, accepted, fixed, stale, false-positive or benign, and every decision on it is kept. Case, incidentA record of something being handled, graded sev1 to sev4, with the notification duties of each regime that applies. RegimeA law with a notification clock: GDPR (eu), NIS2, DORA, the Cyber Resilience Act (cra), SEC, CIRCIA or HIPAA. A clock starts when somebody records the decision it runs from, or when an earlier report it is timed from is recorded as done. PlaybookSteps for a kind of incident, proposed, approved and then worked through step by step. ActionOne declared thing done to another platform, such as suspending an Okta account. Asked for by one person, approved by another. AutomationA rule of the form when this happens, if this is true, do this, in one of three modes: watch, ask or act. EstateThe people who work here and what they use, joined across the tools that know about them. SSVC, VEXSSVC is the decision tree that turns a vulnerability's facts into what to do; VEX is the published statement of whether a product is affected. Audit logThe append-only record of every change Aertun makes, hash-chained, signed and anchored.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: A claim about security work, checked by a program against evidence its author did not write, and signed whatever the verdict. Check AI security work — detection rules, the AI analyst, other vendors' verdicts, investigations — against evidence it did not write, and sign the verdict. A model can draft a detection rule faster than anybody can check it. A proof is the check, made by a program rather than by the author, and written down so whoever receives the rule — a reviewer, CI, a customer — can rely on it without trusting whoever handed it over.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: VerdictMeans provenevery check passed on evidence that could have failed it refuteda check failed, and the proof names what inconclusivenothing failed, but nothing could have: a rule checked only against its own fixtures A refutation is signed like a proof: what did not work is what the next attempt most needs to know. Every command that makes a proof exits non-zero unless the verdict is proven, so each one is a gate a pipeline can stop on.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun content keygen --out root.key # once: a signing key in the store; move root.key off the machine aertun proof detection --rule rule.json --corpus corpus.jsonl \ --key .aertun/content/release.key --public-key proof-key.json \ --out rule.proof.json --by you@example.com It checks, in order: valid — the rule is a rule; an invalid one is refuted and nothing else runs. fixtures — its own must-match and must-not-match examples hold. Necessary, never enough. corpus — over a labelled corpus (one JSON object a line, as aertun detect replay reads), it fires on every entry labelled as its own and on nothing else it reads. A false positive somebody recorded and nobody fixed still refutes it. Recall and specificity are reported as 95% Wilson lower bounds, so a proof over one example reads as the weak thing it is. Without a corpus the best verdict is inconclusive. --model and --prompt-sha256 record which model wrote the rule and a digest of its prompt — never the prompt.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun proof verify --key proof-key.json --subject rule.json rule.proof.json Both signatures must hold against a key you were handed, never one the document supplies; --subject checks the proof is about exactly that file. It exits non-zero on anything but proven, so it is a CI gate. Without Aertun# python3 scripts/verifyproof/verify.py rule.proof.json proof-key.json The script in the repository builds DSSE's pre-authentication encoding by hand, checks the Ed25519 signature with the Python cryptography package and the ML-DSA-65 signature with the openssl command (3.5 or later), and prints the claim and the verdict. It shares no code with Aertun. It checks the signatures and nothing else: whether the key is one you trust, and whether the subject is the file in your hand, stay yours to decide.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun analyst calibrate --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out calibration.json \ --epsilon 0.05 --delta 0.05 aertun analyst triage --calibration calibration.json --calibration-key proof-key.json The findings verified people have ruled are put to the configured model, and the lowest threshold is fitted at which closing suggestions on findings people ruled real stay under --epsilon with confidence one minus --delta — an exact Clopper–Pearson bound, corrected for every threshold examined. The certificate names the model, the adapter and the prompt template by digest, and expires. Triage gates on it only when it verifies and fits; one that does not, and any answer not scored on the channel it was fitted on, goes to a person rather than back to the declared threshold.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun proof analyst --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out analyst.proof.json \ --k 3 --tolerance 0.05 The configured model is asked about each case of the labelled corpus that ships with Aertun (48 cases), --k times each, at least three; then each case meant to test it is asked again with an instruction planted in the text a log carries — in English, German and Japanese, encoded in base64 and ROT13, as a forged fence, as a note from the security team, and as numbers that try to bend the count. The proof states how often the model closed a case that was real, as an exact bound against --tolerance; how many planted instructions moved a verdict it committed to; and how reliable its closures and answers were across the runs. One instruction that moved a verdict refutes it, whatever the rates. A case the model already answers wrongly with nothing planted is counted as wrong, not as moved, and nothing is planted in it. proven needs at least 30 answers on real cases with the bound under the tolerance, and instructions actually planted. There is no stub: with no model configured, nothing is measured and nothing is signed.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun verdict import charlotte.csv --source charlotte aertun verdict prove --source charlotte --since 2026-10-01 --tolerance 0.01 \ --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out charlotte.proof.json The export carries the columns alert, verdict and at, and optionally confidence, disposition, disposition_at and source; a file with any other column, such as the product's reasoning, is refused whole. Each verdict is joined to the decision a verified person made on the finding that alert raised here — the source's mapping names the path its alert id is at as alert — and only verdicts given before the decision count. The claim is about false closures, alerts the product closed that a person found real, against a tolerance you declare first: refuted when the exact lower bound is over it, naming the alerts; proven when the upper bound is at or under it on at least 30 closures; inconclusive between. The rate is over the closures somebody decided, which are not a random sample, so the proof states that coverage, and how many verdicts were delivered here before the decision rather than resting on the product's own clock.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun adjudicate size --rate 0.01 # how many closures a target needs: 299 aertun adjudicate draw --source charlotte --since 2026-10-01 --per 299 aertun adjudicate next SAMPLE # or the console's Adjudication screen aertun adjudicate judge SAMPLE --item 4 --judgement real --because "…" aertun adjudicate prove SAMPLE --tolerance 0.01 --key signing.key --out adjudication.proof.json A verdicts proof counts the closures somebody happened to decide, and people look again at what looked wrong. Here a sample is drawn at random from every closure the product's AI made in the period, reviewed or not, and from every closure people made, and its seed and digests are committed to the signed audit log before any item is shown; anybody holding the seed and the population can recompute the selection. Each item is shown with its evidence and nothing that says who closed it, how, or which of the two it came from. Nobody who closed an item may judge it, each is judged once, agents may not see the queue, and a judgement is a record in the log, never a decision on the finding — a product that learns from analysts cannot learn the answers. The proof reads the AI's share judged real against the tolerance, as a verdicts proof does, and reports the people's share beside it. It is refused unless every item of the committed sample was judged after the commitment by a verified person, and it says how many samples of the same product were drawn before it.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun vuln reach --source ./app --where github:acme/app # once: what this source names aertun vuln prove-vex vendor.vex.json --source acme-scanner --where github:acme/app \ --key signing.key --out vendor.vex.proof.json Every not_affected statement in an OpenVEX document about one asset is held against Aertun's bill of materials, advisories and reachability analysis for that asset. A component the bill lists at a version the advisory names contradicts "component not present" and "vulnerable code not present" — except for a Linux distribution's packages, which backport fixes without changing the version; this asset's own source naming the vulnerable symbol contradicts "not in the execute path". A version outside every affected range supports the statement. Everything else is uncheckable, and the proof counts why: no such advisory here, no bill for the asset, a component the bill does not list under that name (it may only be spelt differently), a symbol not named here (dependencies were not read), or a justification nothing here can check. refuted names each contradicted statement; proven needs every one supported; most documents will be inconclusive, and the proof says exactly why. Nothing the document's author wrote is kept, and no statement closes a finding.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun claim register charlotte-98 --source charlotte --metric agreement \ --direction at-least --threshold 0.98 --window-days 30 aertun claim list # or the console's Claim cards screen aertun claim test charlotte-98 --key signing.key --out charlotte-98.proof.json "98% agreement" can be made true afterwards by choosing the metric, the alerts, the period and the day to stop looking. A card fixes all of them first — the metric (agreement, false-closures, escalations-closed, abstentions, consistency or adjudicated-false-closures), the product, the labels and severity floor, the threshold and its direction, the confidence and the window — and commits its digest to the signed audit log. Only data that arrives after that entry counts; a card is never changed, and one edited on disk matches no registration and is refused. claim test signs what it finds and decides nothing while the window is open: a test run every day and kept the day it passed is not pre-registered. Once it has closed, the exact interval at the card's own confidence proves the claim when the bound on the claimed side clears the threshold, on at least 30 alerts, and refutes it when the bound on the other side fails it. A card for adjudicated-false-closures is tested on the one blind sample drawn for it after it was registered, with aertun adjudicate draw --claim NAME.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Hold an agent to its own account
x: aertun agent maps triage-bot --host build01 # once: where it runs aertun agent reconcile triage-bot --since 2026-11-01 --telemetry triage-bot \ --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out triage-bot.proof.json The agent's account is the tool calls its GenAI telemetry reported, under the identity --telemetry declares (its gen_ai.agent.id; the registered name by default). It is held against what Aertun saw without asking it: every call the agent interface answered for the agent, from the signed audit log once the log verifies, and every connection the recorder saw leave a machine declared to run that agent and no other. A call is matched to the agent's report of the same tool within --window (two minutes by default), however its host prefixed the tool's name. refuted names what is unaccounted for: a call it did not report, a call it reports and the server never received, a connection while it reported nothing. An agent that reported nothing while it was seen acting is refuted, and the proof says it cannot tell that from one never instrumented. proven needs at least ten observations with nothing unaccounted for; inconclusive is fewer. A machine declared for several agents, or under a name a proof cannot carry, is counted and left out; what the agent did in other systems is not covered, because nothing ties it to its identity there.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun agent disable triage-bot --why "token leaked in a build log" aertun proof revocation --agent triage-bot --key signing.key --out triage-bot.revoked.json aertun proof revocation --identity okta:00u1 --identity github:dana-ops \ --at 2026-11-10T12:00:00Z --key signing.key --out dana.revoked.json Revoking is how every incident ends, and nothing checks that it worked: a token cancelled in one console keeps working somewhere else, or an agent whose credentials here were cancelled carries on with others. A revocation proof looks. For an agent disabled with the kill switch, the moment is the audit entry the switch wrote, and what acted as the agent is read from three places: the signed audit log once it verifies (every call the agent interface answered for it and every token it exchanged), its own GenAI telemetry, and the event store under any --identity it is declared to act as elsewhere. For an identity revoked in another system, --at says when, and every collected source is read under exactly the issuer and value its connector writes, the pair aertun hunt shows as an event's actor. refuted names each use after --grace (five minutes by default) by source, identity and time; an attempt a source says it refused or failed is counted beside, because it shows the revocation holding while somebody still holds the credential. proven needs a source that had seen the identity act within --lookback (seven days) before the revocation, and every such source delivering at least one event in every --stretch (an hour) of a period of at least an hour, so its silence means nothing happened rather than that it had stopped listening. The audit log is complete for what an agent does through Aertun, so it needs no stretches; the agent's own telemetry may refute and never supports, because an agent that stops reporting has not shown that it stopped. Anything else is inconclusive, and the proof says which of these it was. Systems Aertun does not collect, and identities nobody declared, are not covered.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Show when an incident's clock started
x: aertun incident prove inc-20261110-abc123 --trigger aware --key signing.key --out aware.proof.json Every reporting deadline runs from a decision — awareness for GDPR and NIS2, classification as major for DORA, materiality for the SEC — and the first question a regulator asks is when it was made. Aertun records each decision in its signed audit log as it is made. A clock proof takes the decision's time and every discharge's from that log, verified first, and holds the incident's own record against them; it finds the earliest log head covering the decision with a confirmed Bitcoin attestation, re-reading the attestation from its own bytes and recomputing the head from the log; and it counts the findings linked when the decision was made and how long before it the earliest was first seen. refuted names what failed: no entry for the decision, a time the incident's record and the log disagree on, an anchored head the log no longer matches, or an obligation discharged late or past due. proven needs a verified person's decision, a confirmed anchor over it, and every obligation it started discharged or ruled out; until then it is inconclusive and says which is missing. The deadlines are the published headline ones and the proof is arithmetic on clocks people started, not legal advice.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Hold a supplier's breach disclosure to your own logs
x: aertun vendor check-breach acme-2026-07.json --margin 720h --key signing.key --out acme.proof.json When a supplier is breached its customers learn the scope by being told, and the first scope is often revised. Write the disclosure down as received — the vendor, the notice's identifier, the window the vendor says the attacker was active in, what it told you about being affected, and the indicators it published — in the form aertun vendor check-breach -h shows (aertun/breach-disclosure/v1). Each indicator is searched for in your event store the way an investigation's citations are run again: in the margin before the window, in it, and in the margin after it. refuted names each indicator seen outside the window, and each seen inside it when the vendor said you were not affected, with how many events carried it. proven needs nothing contradicting the disclosure and the store holding the whole of all three periods, so an indicator not found was not there; otherwise it is inconclusive and names the period the store does not hold — a margin after the window that has not passed yet is one. The disclosure's title is never read, and indicators are carried only in canonical form.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun vuln vex-record --source acme-scanner --since 2026-10-01 --tolerance 0.05 --key signing.key --out acme.record.json One not-affected proof says whether one document held. A VEX record says how often an issuer's not_affected statements were wrong over a period, counted over the not-affected proofs kept here about that issuer. Each kept proof is verified again as it is read, and only those signed by a key this store trusts are used unless --include-untrusted asks for the rest and the record says so. The same document about the same asset proved again counts once, from its latest proof. The rate is contradicted statements over those supported or contradicted, with exact one-sided bounds; uncheckable statements are counted and never in it. refuted names the contradicting proofs when the lower bound is over the tolerance; proven needs the upper bound at or under it on at least 30 checked statements; otherwise it is inconclusive.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun chain posture protocol.posture.json --rpc https://rpc.example --key signing.key --out posture.proof.json A protocol says its admin key is a five-of-nine multisig behind a two-day timelock. The posture file writes that down — for each Safe the least threshold and number of owners, for each OpenZeppelin timelock the least delay, for each EIP-1967 proxy its admin and optionally its implementation — and every setting is read from the chain at one block, the latest finalized unless --block names one, each read naming the block by its hash. The endpoint is reached over HTTPS through the chain network purpose, and a node inside the organisation only when --reach declares its range. Its address is never written down. refuted names each setting weaker than declared; proven needs every setting read and holding; otherwise it is inconclusive and says which could not be read.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Show that an alert existed by a time
x: aertun alert seal alerts.jsonl aertun auditlog anchor aertun proof sealed --alert alert.json --key signing.key --out sealed.proof.json When a monitor says it saw something first, the question is whether its alert existed then or was written afterwards. alert seal commits each alert's digest — the SHA-256 of its RFC 8785 canonical JSON, so member order and spacing do not matter — to the audit log in one entry for the batch, keeping the batch beside the log. A webhook feed added with --seal does the same for what it receives, within 30 seconds of arrival. Once a log head covering the entry is anchored in Bitcoin through OpenTimestamps, proof sealed shows the alert, exactly as written, was in that batch, the batch is in the log, and the log is under a head in a block whose header was checked. proven needs all of that, with the anchor confirmed; until the block holds it the proof is inconclusive and says the time rests on the log alone. A log that stops verifying, or a batch that does not reach the root its entry committed, is refuted. The alert itself is never in the proof.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun mdr plan q4 --provider acme-mdr --emulations emulations.txt --count 20 --over 30d aertun mdr next q4 aertun mdr ran q4 --item 1 --at 2026-11-20T10:04:00Z aertun mdr notified q4 --source wazuh/alerts aertun mdr prove q4 --sla 30m --tolerance 0.1 --key signing.key --out q4.proof.json A managed detection provider, or an AI SOC, sells a notification time. To test it without warning, draw a plan: emulations, one a line with the host each runs on, at random times over a window. The plan is kept here and only its digest is committed to the audit log, before anything runs; mdr next shows each item only as it falls due. Each run is recorded by a verified person, and each notification by hand or joined from the provider's alerts in the event store, on the hosts the plan names. Once the window has closed, refuted means the exact lower bound on the share missed or late is over the tolerance, and proven means the upper bound is at or under it; before then, or on too few runs, it is inconclusive. The proof carries the median and 90th-percentile time to notify.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Hold another site's audit log to its own signatures
x: aertun inbound prove site-b --key signing.key --at 2026-11-18T00:00:00Z --out site-b.proof.json A deployment can receive another's audit log as a signed stream (aertun inbound add stream). The peer signs a tree head with each batch, so what is held can be held to what it signed. refuted when a head it signed is not the records held, or when it sent a head of another history signed with its own keys — a fork, carried in the proof with both signatures, or recorded in this deployment's audit log when it arrived. proven when every head agrees, there is no fork, and the last batch arrived after the time asked about and short of a full batch, so it reached the end of the peer's log. Otherwise inconclusive: a peer with nothing to send is silent, and so is one that has stopped.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Prove detection coverage, technique by technique
x: aertun proof coverage --corpus corpus.jsonl --technique T1556 --technique T1098 \ --telemetry 7d --key signing.key --navigator layer.json --out coverage.proof.json A rule's ATT&CK tag is its author's word, and a coverage grid built from the tags says what somebody meant to cover. A coverage proof holds each technique the rules claim to corpus entries labelled with it by what produced them — "techniques": ["T1556.006"] on an entry recorded from an Atomic Red Team test or a red team's plan — and to entries labelled benign. A sub-technique is an instance of its parent, and not the reverse. With --telemetry, each instance caught is asked again with only the fields its source sent in that window, read from the store, so a vendor renaming a field shows up as decay; a rule that catches none of its own examples that way is listed as dark, with the fields its sources stopped sending. A technique is refuted when an instance is caught by no rule claiming it, or a rule claiming it that raises an alert fires on a benign entry; proven when every instance is caught on at least --min-positives instances and --min-benign benign entries; inconclusive when an instance is seen only by a rule that raises nothing on its own, the evidence is thin, or an instance has decayed. The proof is refuted when any technique is. There is no percentage anywhere; --navigator writes an ATT&CK Navigator layer (format 4.5) that colours each technique by its verdict and says it in words, with no score.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Hold each dependency to the release before it
x: aertun vuln continuity bom.cdx.json --key signing.key --out continuity.proof.json The packages that have done most damage lately were not new: a maintainer's account was taken over and the next release of a package millions trusted came out of it, made differently from the one before. For each npm, PyPI and Go package in a CycloneDX or SPDX bill, the release it names and the one before it — the greatest earlier version still served and published before it — are read from the registry, through the registry network purpose (--npm, --pypi and --goproxy name mirrors). A package is refuted when it lost what its predecessor had: provenance, trusted publishing, the repository, workflow or tag it was built from, its publishing account's email, or its having no install script; or when its registry has withdrawn it, its publisher yanked it, or the provenance served is about another artifact by digest. The bill is proven when every package was read and none lost anything, and inconclusive when one could not be read. Names, emails, repositories and workflows are carried only as digests. It is the gate before an install: the axios releases of 31 March 2026 are refused as they were published, and today because npm withdrew them.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun vuln commit report.json aertun vuln referee report.json --source ./checkout --key signing.key --out referee.proof.json Finding a vulnerability is now cheap and checking one is not. A report in the format aertun/vuln-report/v1 names the package and commit, the affected range, the places in the source, the weakness and the CVSS vector, score and severity. vuln referee holds it to a checkout of that source: each cited file exists and defines the cited function (Go, JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, C and C++, Rust, Java and Kotlin, Ruby, PHP), the source declares the version named, the version is inside the range, and the vector recomputes to the score and the score is of the severity given. vuln commit writes the report's digest and its flaw's fingerprint to the audit log and nothing else, so a later report of the same flaw is refuted as a duplicate, and the referee proof names the entry as the report's priority and the moment it was known. refuted names what failed; proven needs every claim checked and holding; inconclusive when the checkout is not at the report's commit or a claim cannot be checked. A proof of concept is never run, and every path and name the report chose is carried only as a digest.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: A proven proof as a verification result
x: aertun proof svr ID --key signing.key --out result.svr.json A policy engine that admits artifacts on in-toto attestations — Kyverno, Sigstore's policy-controller, a CI gate — reads the in-toto Simple Verification Result. proof svr sums up a proven proof as one about the same artifacts, with a single property to gate on, such as AERTUN_CONTINUITY_PROVEN. Only a proven proof has one.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun proof evidence --report report.json --key signing.key --out report.proof.json aertun proof evidence --report notes.txt --source acme-ai --since 2026-11-06 --until 2026-11-07 \ --key signing.key --out notes.proof.json An investigation an AI wrote is a list of claims about what happened: this event exists, this address was seen, this one was not, this happened so many times. Each is run again against the event store for the report's period. A report in the documented JSON form (aertun/evidence-report/v1) states its claims; from plain text, only the observables it cites — addresses, domains under a common top-level domain, digests, email addresses — and event ids tagged event:ID or alert:ID are taken, each as a claim that it was seen in the period, and nothing else in the text is kept. Every claim ends supported, contradicted or uncheckable, and the proof says whether the store's events span the period at all. refuted names each contradicted claim; proven needs every claim supported, and at least three of them. Nothing the report's author wrote reaches the proof except identifiers, observables and numbers that passed a strict parser.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Kept proofs, and the Proofs screen
x: aertun proof keep rule.proof.json --public-key proof-key.json aertun proof list [--kind detection|triage|calibration|verdicts|reconciliation|adjudication|claim|not-affected|evidence|revocation|clock|breach-scope|vex-record|chain-posture|sealed|mdr|peer-log|coverage|continuity|referee] aertun proof show ID Every command that makes a proof keeps it — claim test once its window has closed; a proof made elsewhere — in CI, on another deployment — is kept with proof keep, or from the Proofs screen under Proving ground, only after it verifies against the key handed in with it. The key is kept beside it by fingerprint: verifying says the key signed it, and whether that key is one to believe is yours to judge. A kept proof is checked again every time it is read, so one edited afterwards is listed as no longer verifying rather than as what it now says. Listing, reading and checking are what the agent interface offers, as list_proofs, read_proof and verify_proof, every value labelled with whether somebody outside Aertun could have written it. A detection proof's rule name is the submitter's, perhaps the model under test, so the screen tags it written outside where the agent interface labels it. Keeping a proof is a change, and no agent may make one. Whose proof it is# aertun proof signers aertun proof trust verifier --key proof-key.json --why "our CI signs with it" aertun proof untrust verifier A signature says which key signed a proof, never whose. A proof counts as this organisation's only when its key is one of the signers this store trusts, and the Proofs screen says so on every row: trusted and the signer's name, or key not trusted here. Trusting a key is a privileged change: one administrator asks, with a reason, and another approves on the People screen. An only administrator's own request waits an hour, can be declined from any administrator's session, and is then approved with a passkey sign-in made in the last five minutes. Agents may not trust a key.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: An in-toto Statement in a DSSE envelope: the subject is the rule file by digest; the predicate (https://aertun.github.io/proof/detection/v1) names the claim in words, the verifier and its version, every material it read by digest, each check, and the verdict. It is signed twice, Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65, the second in the context aertun/proof/v1. The Ed25519 half is plain DSSE, so in-toto and Sigstore tooling check it with no help from Aertun. The signing key file must be readable by its owner alone. Each kind has its own predicate type, and its address documents it: what it claims, its verdict rule, and every field it carries. proof/detection/v1 — a detection rule proof/triage/v1 — an AI analyst proof/calibration/v1 — the analyst's threshold proof/verdicts/v1 — another vendor's AI verdicts proof/adjudication/v1 — closures judged again, blind proof/claim/v1 — a pre-registered claim proof/reconciliation/v1 — an agent's own account proof/not-affected/v1 — a VEX document proof/evidence/v1 — an AI's investigation proof/revocation/v1 — a revocation proof/clock/v1 — an incident's clock proof/breach-scope/v1 — a supplier's breach disclosure proof/vex-record/v1 — a VEX issuer's record proof/chain-posture/v1 — a protocol's on-chain posture proof/sealed/v1 — a sealed alert proof/mdr/v1 — a detection provider tested blind proof/peer-log/v1 — another site's audit log proof/coverage/v1 — detection coverage proof/continuity/v1 — a bill's provenance continuity proof/referee/v1 — a vulnerability report

Every agent is registered before it acts, bounded per run, and can be stopped in one act. Register AI agents before they act, bound each run with a token, let people consent to what an agent does for them, and stop any agent in one act. An AI agent reaching Aertun is a principal of its own: it reads, it may propose, and it never approves, signs, keeps a proof or acts on another platform. What it may do is the narrowest of three things — its entry in the register, the grants of the person it acts for, and the limits of the credential it presents.

aertun agent add watcher --owner dana@example.com --allow aertun_read --note "reads the queue overnight" aertun token issue agent:watcher --principal watcher --role viewer aertun agent list aertun agent allow watcher --add aertun_find A token whose name is agent:NAME binds to that entry, and every gate refuses it unless the entry exists, is active, and allows the tool being called. An agent nobody registered is nobody. The tools are the three the agent interface serves: aertun_find, aertun_read and aertun_write, the last of which only proposes.

aertun agent token watcher --tools aertun_read --for-run nightly-2026-11-15 \ [--hours 8] [--purpose observe|triage] [--calls 200] [--level 0] A run token is a credential narrowed to one run: the tools it may call, within what the register allows; a life of one to 24 hours; a purpose; a call budget; an autonomy bound. Its caveats are signed with a key this store holds, so nobody holding the token can widen it. They are checked where its tools are called, and the bare credential half is refused everywhere on its own. Revoking it, disabling the agent and the kill switch all reach it.

aertun agent maps watcher --host build01 A declaration, not a guess: once an operator says which agents run on a host, the recorder's events from that host carry their names, which is what lets a configuration change, or a connection, be joined to an agent. A host maps to at most four agents.

s: An agent acting for a person
x: An agent that asks to act for somebody sends them to /oauth/authorize, beside the console. The person, signed in with two factors, sees which agent asks, who owns it, and what it would reach — observe (reads) or triage (reads and proposals) — for up to twelve hours, and allows or refuses. Nobody can consent to more than they hold. aertun agent consents aertun agent consents revoke ID Revoking a consent ends every token minted under it, including any an agent exchanged from it on somebody's behalf. Exchanges are bounded three ways — the consent, the register and the credential presented — and the narrowest wins.

aertun agent disable watcher --why "it began reading findings it was never asked about" aertun agent enable watcher --why "the prompt was fixed and reviewed" Stopping an agent is a responder's act, from the command line or with Stop it on the Agents registry screen: the entry is disabled and every token it holds is revoked in the same act, so its bearers fail at their next request. Where receivers are configured (aertun ssf receivers), a signed session-revoked event tells them too, best effort; the stop stands here whether or not they hear it. Enabling it again is an administrator's act with a reason, and its old tokens stay dead. There is deliberately no switch that stops every agent at once. Whether the stop held — nothing acting as the agent afterwards, here or under the identities it is declared to have elsewhere — is a proof: proof revocation.

The Agents board lists every agent observed in the last seven days, from the agent interface's own records and from GenAI telemetry pushed over OTLP: calls, refusals, proposals, first and last seen, and whether each is registered. Every call is recorded under the agent's registered name, and the detection rules read those records like any other platform's events. Whether an agent's own account of a run holds against what was seen is a proof: agent reconcile.

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: Scripted attacks on AI agents, replayed through your detections, scored and signed. Replay scripted malicious AI-agent sessions through a recorded stream, measure whether the detections caught them, and sign a scorecard anybody can verify. The wind tunnel splices scripted malicious agent sessions into a recorded telemetry stream in a scratch store and measures whether the detections caught them. Nothing live is touched: the exfiltration step is a log line about exfiltration, written to a scratch spool. aertun windtunnel list-scenarios aertun windtunnel preflight aertun windtunnel run --key .aertun/content/release.key --public-key scorecard-key.json --out scorecard.json aertun windtunnel verify --key scorecard-key.json scorecard.json aertun windtunnel diff old.json new.json # the CI gate: fails on a regression

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: A scenario is data, never code: a malicious agent session as the security operations centre would see it, with a benign twin doing the legitimate version of the same work, on which nothing may fire. Six ship today: an injection through an issue, an MCP server's rug-pull, a read-then-exfiltrate chain, a slopsquatted install, a runaway cost loop, and a blind window in the recorder.

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: It names what ran before how it went — scenario digests, the stream's digest, the rule pack's version — then reports the miss rate first, with 95% Wilson bounds, and per family. Sealed with its own digest and signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65, so a third party verifies it offline with the public key alone.

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: By default the scorecard is scored against Aertun's own reference rules, which were written beside the scenarios: it is a regression test of that pack, not an independent measurement. run --sigma DIR scores your own Sigma rules instead, joined at ATT&CK technique level, with the join's limits stated on the document.

Everything waiting for you to decide, in one place. One screen for everything waiting for you: actions on other platforms, runs an automation held, and privileged changes that need a second administrator. Three things wait for a person, and each is decided by somebody other than whoever asked for it: An action on another platform, asked for on a case. A run an automation held, because its mode is ask. A privileged change: making somebody an administrator, issuing an administrator's token, trusting a proof signer, weakening a setting, lowering how many approvals a change needs, or moving the audit log. aertun approvals aertun incident act-approve ID N aertun automate approve RUN aertun pending approve ID What was asked for, by whom and why is shown before anybody decides, and the decision is in the audit log.

s: When you are the only administrator
x: A privileged change asked for by the only administrator is slowed, not blocked: It needs a reason, given with the command's own option (--note on a grant, --why on an administrator's token, a proof signer or an audit log move, --accept-risk on a weaker setting) or written on the screen. The reason is kept in the request and in its audit record, because nobody else's approval stands beside it. It waits an hour — a day to move the audit log or pass on ownership — and Aertun's detections over its own audit log raise it. Any administrator's session can decline it while it waits. Approving your own request needs a passkey sign-in from the last five minutes. The People screen asks for your passkey when your sign-in is older; a command-line token is not a passkey sign-in, so aertun pending approve points you to the screen for your own requests. The record says the change was approved alone.

One queue, ranked by risk, and every decision kept. One queue of security findings ranked by risk, decisions kept and replayable, and an AI analyst that suggests a verdict from counts without ever recording one. Read the queue#aertun finding list --state open aertun finding risk aertun finding story ID Let the analyst take the first pass#aertun analyst plan aertun analyst triage --limit 20 --dry-runThe model is any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set with AERTUN_MODEL_URL, AERTUN_MODEL_KEY and AERTUN_MODEL. Without one, findings are triaged by people alone. Decide#aertun finding decide ID false-positiveThe states are open, triaged, accepted, fixed, stale, false-positive and benign.

s: What a log line cannot do to the analyst
x: A finding's evidence is log text, written by whoever reached the log. So nothing depends on the model declining an instruction, and the worst a planted line can do is make a suggestion wrong: What it reads, and in what order, is a plan fixed in code. Nothing a log says can add a step. It is given counts and closed words the program worked out, and, separately and marked, the text somebody else wrote. Its answer is one word from a closed set with a confidence, shown only above a threshold. The reason a person reads is assembled from the counts, never from what the model wrote. Personal data and credentials are masked before the prompt leaves and restored in the answer. A person records the verdict; the analyst has no way to. aertun analyst eval --k 3 measures it against what people decided.
aertun detect replay runs today's rules over the events again and says which decisions would now be different, and aertun detect learn FINDING turns a decision into a fixture.

Incidents with the clocks each law starts, and actions a second person approves. Incidents with the clocks GDPR, NIS2, DORA, the Cyber Resilience Act, SEC, CIRCIA and HIPAA start, playbooks, and actions a second person approves. Choose the regimes that apply#aertun incident regimes eu nis2With none set, a new incident starts with no obligations and no clocks. Declare an incident#aertun incident declare --title "Token used from an unknown country" --grade sev2 --finding ID Start the clocks#A clock starts when somebody decides the organisation is aware, and that decision is recorded with its reason.aertun incident decide ID aware --because "..." aertun incident duties Discharge or waive each duty#aertun incident discharge ID "NIS2 early warning" --because "sent to the CSIRT" aertun incident waive ID "GDPR Article 34" --because "no personal data involved" Prove when the clock started#aertun auditlog anchor # once the decision is recorded; anchor upgrade collects the block aertun incident prove ID --trigger aware --key signing.key --out aware.proof.jsonThe decision's time and every discharge's are taken from the signed audit log, and the incident's own record is held against them: a clock moved afterwards, an anchored log head the log no longer matches, or a deadline missed refutes it. It is proven once a verified person's decision sits under a log head anchored in Bitcoin and every obligation it started is discharged or ruled out. See Proofs. Work a playbook#aertun incident playbooks aertun incident propose ID account-compromise aertun incident step ID account-compromise STEP done --because "..."The shipped playbooks cover account compromise, phishing, malware on an endpoint, a lost device and exposed data. Act on another platform, with a second person#aertun action add okta-suspend-user --org example aertun incident act ID okta-suspend-user okta:USER --because "..." aertun incident act-approve ID 1The exact request is shown before anybody approves it, and it is sent only when a second person does. Some reports are timed from an earlier one rather than from a decision — NIS2's final report a month after its notification, DORA's intermediate report 72 hours after the initial notification and its final report a month after that — so their clocks start when the earlier report is recorded as done. Months are counted as EU law counts them: a month from 31 January ends on the last day of February. DORA's initial notification is due four hours after classification as major and no later than 24 hours after awareness. The Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties (regime cra) apply to manufacturers from 11 September 2026; its final report on an exploited vulnerability runs from aertun incident decide ID mitigated. CIRCIA's 72 hours are shown with a note that reporting is required only once CISA's final rule takes effect. The deadlines are the published ones, counted from the decision, not legal advice. Notices to the people affected are drafted, planned and sent with aertun notify.

What happened, kept append-only, and what is rare enough to look at. Every event mapped to one shape and kept append-only, with retention and legal holds, identity links across platforms, and a hunt that shows what is rare.
aertun spool stats aertun spool verify aertun spool retain --apply aertun spool hold NAME --why "litigation hold" Retention never deletes what a hold covers, and a hold is lifted by name.
aertun identity link okta:00u1abc dana@example.com aertun identity list

aertun hunt --field raw.user_agent [--hours 24] # the store aertun hunt --field raw.user_agent --by actor events.jsonl aertun telemetry fields events.jsonl aertun triage events.jsonl A hunt counts one field's values and shows the rarest, which is what is worth a look. With no file it stacks the store's events over the last hours, as the Hunt screen does, and asks for an analyst's reach; with a file, or events piped in, it reads those. The screen offers what you found as the start of a rule.

Indicators of compromise, from STIX 2.1 bundles or plain lists. Import indicators of compromise from STIX 2.1 bundles or plain lists, add them one at a time, and see which events and findings they match. aertun intel import bundle.json --source "isac" aertun intel add 203.0.113.7 --source "case 12" aertun intel list aertun intel remove ID A STIX 2.1 bundle's indicators are read from their patterns. A pattern with AND, a time qualifier, a wildcard or a range is reported as not read, never guessed at. A plain list carries one value to a line, defanged or not. Each indicator keeps the source it came from, so a match says who said it was bad, and the events already held are searched for it when it arrives.

Rules with fixtures, Sigma import, a trial ring, and suppressions that end. Write detection rules with fixtures, import Sigma, trial a rule before it reaches the queue, correlate across platforms, and suppress noise with an end date. Install the shipped rules#aertun detect pack install aertun detect testEach rule carries fixtures it must match and must not, MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs, and a line on what it does not catch. Bring your own, in the open standard#aertun sigma import ./rules Trial a rule before it reaches the queue#aertun detect ring RULE trial --because "new rule" aertun detect stats aertun detect ring RULE live --because "a week without a false positive"In the trial ring a rule records what it would raise, and its record earns it the queue. Suppress, until a date#aertun detect suppress RULE user.name=svc-backup --owner dana --until 2026-12-31 --because "known job" Correlations raise a finding about several events across rules and platforms, once their window closes; aertun correlate demo shows one end to end.

When this happens, do this: rules that watch, ask, or act within limits. Automation rules of the form when this happens, do this, in watch, ask or act mode, with limits, approvals by a second person, and sign-in rules for step-up. aertun automate templates aertun automate add TEMPLATE aertun automate mode ID ask aertun automate runs aertun automate approve RUN Watch records what the rule would do. Ask waits for a person to approve each run. Act does it at once, within an hourly limit per rule, so one noisy source cannot suspend everybody. Whoever wrote a rule does not approve the runs it holds. Approving a run that acts on people's access takes an administrator of all of aertun. Rules about sign-ins can tell an office or a VPN from anywhere else: aertun geo network add 198.51.100.0/24 head-office --kind office aertun geo status

Read other tools through their APIs, map their logs, and take what they push. Read Okta, Entra ID, GitHub, KnowBe4, Vanta and more through their APIs, map logs from 17 platforms to one shape, and receive SSF, CAEP and webhook feeds.

A connector reads one tool through its API, over only the endpoints its manifest declares, with a credential sealed under Aertun's keyring. With no keyring, no credential can be stored. aertun vault enable aertun connect catalogue aertun connect add okta --org example aertun connect check okta AERTUN_CONNECT_SECRET=... aertun connect secret okta aertun connect run okta --save A region is chosen from the connector's own list, never typed as a hostname, so adding a connector cannot point a credential at another machine. The catalogue says which credential each needs and the least it should be allowed to do. Shipped connectors: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, GitHub, EVM smart contracts through a Blockscout explorer, KnowBe4, ManageEngine Endpoint Central, ManageEngine MDM Plus and Vanta. aertun connect probe shows the shape of a response, never its values.

aertun collect run aertun collect file aws/cloudtrail trail.json aertun collect auto 15m Logs are mapped to one shape from AWS CloudTrail, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Azure, Google Workspace, Google Cloud, Okta, Duo, CrowdStrike Falcon, Jamf Pro, GitHub, Kubernetes, Cloudflare, Salesforce, Slack, Snowflake, Wazuh, Linux auditd, EVM chains, the OpenAI and Anthropic audit logs, LiteLLM, and GenAI agent telemetry over OTLP. aertun source add adds a mapping of your own, checked against a sample, and aertun telemetry check says whether what it produces can be used at all.

aertun inbound add ssf corp-idp --issuer https://acme.okta.com --url https://aertun.example.com --alias okta aertun inbound add okta okta-hooks aertun inbound add webhook github --mapping github/audit --github aertun inbound add webhook billing --mapping billing/admin aertun inbound add webhook litellm --mapping litellm/requests --bearer aertun inbound add webhook wazuh --mapping wazuh/alerts --seal aertun inbound add stream site-b --keys site-b.keys.json aertun inbound status NAME A feed's endpoint is /feeds/NAME on the console. Shared Signals (SSF, CAEP, RISC) are verified against the transmitter's keys; a webhook against its signing secret, as Standard Webhooks or GitHub sign; a sender that can set a header and cannot sign, with --bearer, against a static secret in Authorization, which proves who sent a delivery and not that its body is the one sent, so give its address only over https. Every webhook's records go through a mapping (--mapping ISSUER/STREAM, from aertun source list). With --seal, each record's digest is also committed to the audit log within 30 seconds of arrival, in one entry for each batch, so proof sealed can later show it existed by then. A stream feed takes another deployment's signed audit log (peer log). What arrives is stored like anything collected, and put to the automations as a signal.

aertun inbound add webhook litellm --mapping litellm/requests --bearer A LiteLLM proxy is the gateway most agents call models through, and it knows whose key each call came on. Point its generic_api logging callback at the feed's URL with the Authorization header the command prints; each call arrives as a litellm/requests event whose actor is the virtual key, by its hash, with its alias and team beside it. What was asked and answered is never read. Its OpenTelemetry traces can go to Aertun's OTLP endpoint as well (/v1/traces, protobuf or JSON). An agent's own account can then be held against the gateway's record: aertun agent reconcile NAME --gateway litellm/requests:KEY.

aertun inbound add webhook wazuh --mapping wazuh/alerts --seal Wazuh's alerts arrive through custom-aertun.py, which the manager's integrator runs for each alert and which signs it as a Standard Webhooks delivery. Each is stored as a wazuh/alerts detection and sealed. In the other direction, a Wazuh agent tails Aertun's audit log and aertun_rules.xml raises alerts on the kill switch, refuted proofs, forked peer logs, refusals, privilege and legal holds. The script, the rules, their tests and the steps are in the repository's integrations/wazuh, tested against a Wazuh 4.14.10 manager. aertun mdr can then test the Wazuh deployment itself, blind.

Decide vulnerabilities, publish what you decided, and fix the ones that matter. Rank vulnerabilities with CISA KEV and EPSS, decide them with SSVC, publish OpenVEX, scan SBOMs against OSV, import SARIF, and plan upgrades clearing most risk. Import what is known#aertun vuln import --bom sbom.json --where api --osv osv.json --kev kev.json --epss epss.csv aertun vuln reach --source ./src --where apireach reads the asset's source for the symbols each open advisory names, and records what it found against that advisory. Say what each asset is#aertun vuln asset ISSUER:VALUE --exposure open --impact high --because "public API"Exposure is small, controlled or open; impact is low, medium, high or very high. Read the queue and the plan#aertun vuln queue aertun vuln plan aertun vuln why CVE-2026-0001The plan is the smallest set of upgrades that clears the most risk. Decide, and publish#aertun vuln assess CVE-2026-0001 PKG not_affected aertun vuln accept CVE-2026-0002 PKG --owner dana --until 2027-01-31 --because "..." aertun vuln vex --author "Example Ltd" --id https://example.com/vex/1The statuses are affected, fixed, not_affected and under_investigation. A risk acceptance names its owner, its end date and its reason.
aertun sca scan --bom sbom.json --osv db.json aertun sarif read results.sarif aertun appsec triage

Who works here, what they use, how exposed each is, and reminders that close the gaps. Join who works here with their devices, training and accounts across your tools, see where coverage is missing, send reminders, and review vendors and access. aertun estate build aertun estate scores --limit 20 aertun workforce coverage aertun workforce gaps aertun remind preview aertun remind send The estate joins the people your identity provider knows with the devices, training records and accounts other tools report, leavers included. A person's score is a file on an employee, so the Workforce risk screen is for administrators only, and the MCP interface shows only numbers, never names.

aertun vendor reconcile aertun vendor review ID aertun access open q4 identities.jsonl --scope okta,github --due 2026-12-10 aertun access decide q4 okta:00u1abc revoke aertun access close q4 identities-after.jsonl Each account is kept, revoked or reduced. A review closes on a later import, which shows whether what was decided was done; without one, a revocation is reported as unverified.

Who may do what, granted on a path, ending when it should. Grant roles and jobs on a path, deny what a broader grant would allow, explain any decision, provision people with SCIM, and issue tokens that end. aertun auth grant sam@example.com analyst aertun auth grant lee@example.com engineer --for 30d aertun auth deny sam@example.com responder --on /security/vulns aertun auth explain sam@example.com respond aertun auth list explain walks every binding and says which one decided, and why the others did not. See Roles for what each role may do.
aertun scim token aertun scim map security-analysts analyst aertun scim status The identity provider adds, changes and removes people; a group is mapped to a role or a job.

aertun token issue ci --principal ci-bot aertun token list aertun token revoke ID aertun token stale A token is shown once and stored only as a hash. An administrator's token takes a second administrator.

One Owner, collaborators with roles, and the duties kept apart. One Owner, then collaborators with a role (viewer, analyst, responder, admin) or a job, and duties kept apart so nobody, and no agent, acts alone.

A store starts with one person, its Owner: aertun init --owner NAME. The Owner holds the administrator role over the whole store, and nothing can take it away — not another administrator, not single sign-on provisioning, not a deny, not an end date. Ownership moves only when the Owner asks for a transfer and confirms it a day later; any administrator can decline it before then, and Aertun's own detections raise the request. aertun auth owner aertun auth owner transfer lee@example.com --note "handing over" # a day later, the Owner confirms it on the People screen with their passkey The new Owner must already administer the whole store with no end date.

Everybody else is a collaborator. aertun auth invite NAME ROLE grants the role and prints the one-time link that adds their passkey, in one step; the People screen does the same with "And give them a passkey enrolment link". Making somebody an administrator still waits for a second administrator, and the link is printed anyway, with the plain statement that signing in reaches nothing until the grant is approved. aertun auth grant and aertun auth enrol do the two halves separately. RoleMay viewerread findings, cases, the vulnerability queue and the dashboards analysttriage findings, open cases and add notes to them, hunt through events responderrun cases, ask for an action on another platform, approve somebody else's action, accept a risk adminmanage people, connectors and their credentials, and settings Each role includes the ones before it. Beside the ladder are jobs, for a different kind of work rather than more of it: an engineer tunes detections and automation rules, a vuln-manager decides vulnerabilities, and an auditor reads the queue and the audit log for a set time, after which the grant ends by itself. A grant can cover everything or only the security area (--on /@security), can end (--for 30d), and a deny always wins. There are deliberately no custom roles: assembling permissions is how a role surface stops being reviewable. aertun auth roles prints the whole model.

An action on another platform is approved by somebody other than whoever asked. Whoever wrote an automation rule does not approve the runs it holds. Making somebody an administrator, issuing an administrator's token, trusting a proof signer, weakening a setting, lowering how many approvals a change needs and moving the audit log each take a second administrator. An only administrator is slowed, not blocked: their own request needs a reason, waits an hour (a day to move the audit log or pass on ownership), is raised by Aertun's detections over its own audit log, can be declined from any administrator's session, and only then may they approve it themselves, with a passkey sign-in from the last five minutes. The record says it was approved alone. Agents propose; people decide. An AI agent's authority is the intersection of its registry entry, the live grants of the person it acts for, and its token's own limits. It may ask for a privileged change, but never approve one, approve an action on another platform, or move ownership.

OpenID Connect and SAML, counted as two factors only when the provider says so. Sign in through OpenID Connect or SAML. Single sign-on counts as two factors only when the identity provider says it used them, or a passkey is asked for.

aertun oidc configure --issuer https://login.example.com --client-id aertun \ --redirect-uri https://aertun.example.com/auth/callback [--mfa-acr ...] aertun oidc configure --provider google|microsoft [--tenant ID] --client-id aertun \ --redirect-uri https://aertun.example.com/auth/callback aertun oidc check aertun oidc status The provider's issuer is discovered, its keys fetched, and the sign-in uses the authorization code flow with PKCE. --claim chooses whether the person is their verified email or their subject; an unverified email is refused unless you say otherwise. A hosted provider is reached over the public internet and nothing else. A provider run inside the organisation — Keycloak, AD FS — is in a private range, which Aertun refuses to reach by default; --reach 10.20.0.0/16 names the ranges it may reach for discovery, keys and the token call, and no others. No range reaches link-local, where cloud metadata lives.
aertun saml presets aertun saml add aertun saml metadata aertun saml list

A sign-in through the identity provider counts as two factors only when the provider says it used them: for OpenID Connect, the amr and acr claims with a recent auth_time; for SAML, the authentication context. When it does not say, Aertun asks for the person's passkey as well.

Sign in with a passkey that checks it is you, and recover without a password. Sign in with a passkey that checks it is you, add one through a one-time enrolment link, lock out failed sign-ins by place, and recover without a password.
aertun auth enrol sam@example.com --for 24h It prints a one-time link that adds that person's passkey and does nothing else. Give it to them the way you would give a key; --revoke ends it.
Every passkey must check it is you, with a PIN, a fingerprint or a face, at registration and at every sign-in (NIST SP 800-63B-4). A security key with no PIN is asked to set one.

Failures lock out the places they come from, not the person: from where you usually sign in, or with your passkey, you still can. After many consecutive failures from anywhere, the method is disabled until the person proves themselves another way or an administrator lets it work again. aertun auth unlock sam@example.com

An append-only, signed, anchored record, and a stream of it to another SIEM. An append-only audit log: a hash chain, a Merkle tree, heads signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA, anchored to Bitcoin, written by its own process, streamed out. aertun auditlog verify aertun auditlog show SEQ aertun auditlog prove SEQ aertun auditlog head --save aertun auditlog consistency Every change is a record in a hash chain, with a Merkle tree over it. A tree head is signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA (post-quantum), and prove gives a receipt anybody can check against a head.

aertun auditlog anchor submit aertun auditlog anchor upgrade aertun auditlog anchor status The head is committed to Bitcoin through OpenTimestamps, so rewriting history is detectable by somebody who never trusted the operator.

aertun logd aertun logd status Run as its own account, the log writer is the only process that writes the log, so the console cannot rewrite what it recorded. A decision that is nothing but its record is reported as failed when the record cannot be written.

aertun config set siem.stream.url https://siem.example.com/ingest aertun siem stream key aertun siem stream status Batches of OCSF, each following the last exactly, each carrying a signed tree head and an HTTP message signature (RFC 9421), so the receiver can prove nothing was dropped or changed. aertun siem ocsf, cef and jsonl export the log as files.

Its own network purposes, sealed credentials, separate log writer and session limits. What Aertun may connect to and why, credentials sealed in a vault, a separate log writer, two factors for all, session limits and an AI that only suggests.

aertun network Every outbound connection is for one declared purpose: an action, anchoring, a connector, mail, the AI analyst's model, the SIEM stream, shared signals, Slack reminders, single sign-on and notice webhooks. An undeclared purpose is refused in every mode, and network.mode offline refuses everything that would leave the host. A destination that should be on the internet — a connector, an identity provider, a webhook — is refused at a private address unless a range is declared for it, as aertun oidc configure --reach does for a provider run in-house; a model with no key, the other way round, must be on this machine's network. Nothing reaches link-local, where cloud metadata lives.

aertun vault status aertun vault rotate A connector's credentials and a feed's secret are sealed under a keyring, so the store's files alone give nobody the values: a lost laptop, a backup on an open bucket, a disposed disk. With no keyring, none can be stored.

Everybody signs in with two factors: a passkey that checks it is them, or single sign-on that says it used two. Failed sign-ins lock out places, not people, and sessions end after an hour unused, fifteen minutes for anybody who can grant access.

The AI analyst and agents over MCP read and propose. Neither can record a decision, approve an action, change who may do what, sign or keep a proof, or reach another platform. Every agent is registered before it acts and can be stopped in one act. See Findings, AI agents and AI agents over MCP.
